about: Every promise IronDome makes, the boundary of that promise, and the tests that hold it. `tests` are pytest node ids in this repository; `selfcheck` names the check `irondome verify` runs on your own machine. tests/claims/test_registry.py fails the build if a claim has no test, if a listed test does not exist, if a claim's own test file has a test that is not listed, if the README, the threat model, the architecture or SECURITY.md refers to a claim this file does not have, or if the README's sample session shows output the program does not print; scripts/site_data.py --check fails the website's build if its copy of this file differs.

closed_limits.L1: 3.x: key protection was software-only (no TPM, no Secure Enclave).
closed_limits.L2: 3.x: the biometric check was an OS gate in front of a readable key, not cryptographic.
closed_limits.L3: 3.x: nuke could not defeat an SSD controller (overwrite, fsync, unlink).
closed_limits.L4: 3.x: the key was never zeroed in memory (immutable bytes inside a Fernet object).
closed_limits.L5: 3.x: the cipher was AES-128-CBC (Fernet splits its 32-byte key into a 16-byte AES key and a 16-byte HMAC key).

claims.title: A copy of the vault is useless without the machine
claims.statement: Every keyslot opened by a master password or a fingerprint also needs a device secret that is not in the vault file. A complete copy of the vault directory, together with the correct master password, does not open on another machine and gives an attacker nothing to test password guesses against.
claims.boundary: The recovery key is exempt by design: it exists to open the vault without the device. With the file-based backend the device secret is a file in a separate directory: it protects copies of the vault, not a machine that malware already controls.

claims.title: On an Apple-silicon Mac or Linux with a TPM 2.0, the device secret is held by the security chip
claims.statement: macOS on Apple silicon: the device secret is the result of a key agreement with a P-256 private key that is generated inside the Secure Enclave and never leaves it; a key blob from any other Secure Enclave is rejected. Linux: the device secret is stored in a TPM 2.0 NV index and appears nowhere on disk.
claims.boundary: Needs the Secure Enclave of an Apple-silicon Mac, or a TPM 2.0 the user may access. Intel Macs, T2 chip or not, are untested and not supported: cryptography publishes no macOS wheel for them, so installing there builds it from source, which needs Rust and OpenSSL. Without a chip, IronDome uses the file-based backend and says so in `irondome status`. Windows has no hardware backend yet.

claims.title: Touch ID is enforced by the Secure Enclave, not by IronDome
claims.statement: A keyslot under the biometry policy uses a Secure Enclave key created with the biometryCurrentSet access control. The chip refuses the key operation until its sensor reports a match for a currently enrolled finger. Asked to operate without user interaction, the key produces no secret: the operation fails with 'authentication is required to use this key'.
claims.boundary: macOS only. The automated suite proves the refusal; the acceptance needs a finger and is checked with `irondome verify --touch`. Adding or removing a fingerprint invalidates the key (use the master password or recovery key, then enrol again). The prompt names the helper program, not the caller.

claims.title: On Linux the TPM checks the password and rate-limits guesses
claims.statement: The TPM verifies a value derived from the master password before releasing the device secret, with dictionary-attack protection enabled on the NV index: a wrong password is refused by the chip, and repeated failures put the TPM into lockout.
claims.boundary: The lockout is the TPM's global dictionary-attack counter; its thresholds are set by the machine's TPM configuration, not by IronDome. The counter does not know who is guessing: any program running as you, a process that holds only a grant included, can use up the allowance and lock the owner out until the TPM forgives the failures. A TPM in lockout takes no new keyslot either; `irondome recovery use` then names the way in with a file-based device key.

claims.title: nuke makes every copy of the vault directory unreadable
claims.statement: nuke destroys the device secrets before it deletes anything else: the one every keyslot opened by a password or a fingerprint needs, and the one every session and grant is bound to. Afterwards, restoring a complete, bit-perfect copy of the vault directory and supplying the correct master password, a session token or a grant token opens nothing: what an SSD kept of the old blocks no longer matters.
claims.boundary: A recovery key on paper can still open a surviving copy of the vault file; nuke says so when the vault has one. A portable backup made with irondome export needs no device secret and opens with its own password. TPM: the secret was only ever inside the chip. Secure Enclave: what is deleted is the sealed key blob, a file in the device directory, and a copy of that file works again in this Mac's Secure Enclave (under Touch ID, with a finger) and nowhere else. So the statement is about copies of the vault directory: a backup, clone or snapshot that also holds the device directory, put back on this Mac, opens the vault with the master password or with a token that was valid when the copy was made. IronDome marks the device directory as left out of Time Machine when it creates it; a clone, a disk image, a local snapshot or a backup program that does not read the mark is not kept from copying it. The mark was read back with macOS's own tools; no Time Machine backup was run to see it honoured. File-based backend: the device key file is overwritten and unlinked, which on an SSD is best effort, and a copy of the device directory opens the vault in the same way.

claims.title: Key material is wiped from memory
claims.statement: IronDome keeps its copies of the master password, the prehash it derives from it, the Argon2id output, the device secret, the key-encryption key, the vault key and every subkey only in memory outside the Python heap, locked into RAM where the system allows it, and overwrites them when the vault is locked. Argon2id is never given the master password: IronDome first derives 32 bytes from it with HKDF-SHA256, the prehash, and Argon2id stretches those. Argon2id does not run in IronDome's own process: a child process made for that one derivation is sent the prehash through a pipe, sends the key back and exits, and the key is read straight into IronDome's buffer. HKDF writes its output straight into IronDome's buffers and is run a second time with an all-zero key, so that what the library leaves behind of the first run is overwritten by the second. After a full session, a scan of the process's entire address space finds no copy of any of them; right after the first derivation a process makes, a search finds no part of an ASCII master password of up to 4,000 bytes.
claims.boundary: pyca/cryptography and the OpenSSL it bundles copy what Argon2id is given into memory they free without overwriting. Argon2id is given the prehash, so the copy is of the prehash. By itself the prehash opens nothing but this one keyslot: with the vault file and the device it opens the vault as the password would, and for a portable backup written by `irondome export`, whose keyslot has no device secret, the backup file alone is enough. Whoever reads it and knows the keyslot's salt, which is in the vault file, can also test guesses of the master password against it at the speed of SHA-256, with no device and no TPM counting wrong guesses; a password found that way opens whatever that password protects. IronDome cannot prevent that copy and does not write to the library's memory itself; it has Argon2id run in a child process, so the copy is made in memory that ends with the child, a moment after the key is sent back. For as long as the derivation takes, the child's memory holds the prehash and the key outside locked pages, and the key crosses a pipe on its way back. Where no child can be made, Argon2id runs in IronDome's own process: when another thread is running in it, when the system refuses to fork, and where there is no fork. None of IronDome's own commands stretches a password with a second thread running. In that case IronDome runs Argon2id a second time on zeros, and the library, asking for blocks of the same sizes, may be handed the ones it just freed and overwrite the copy. That is the allocator's choice, not a guarantee: with glibc the tests found no copy left; macOS's allocator, where it does not zero what it frees (macOS 15 on GitHub's machines, or any macOS with MallocZeroOnFree=0), left the copy of the prehash in most runs, and a copy that is left lasts until that memory is reused. The master password itself is given only to HKDF, which reads it a block at a time. For an ASCII password of up to 4,000 bytes the tests find no copy of it afterwards, whole or in part. They search for it in pieces: 16 bytes over its last 512, 32 or 64 before that, so a copy shorter than two pieces can be missed; a review before release searched for any 8 bytes of it, through `init`, unlocking, a wrong password and `export`, and found none. The tests' control gives Argon2id the password in the probe's own process, as IronDome did before both things were changed, and the same search then finds the end of a long password on Linux and, in most runs, all of it on macOS with zeroing off. The control is part of the test suite, not of `irondome verify`. That HKDF leaves no copy of its input is how this version of the library works, measured on Linux with glibc and on macOS, both on arm64; IronDome does not control it. `irondome migrate` has to give the password of a 3.x vault to that format's own PBKDF2; the review found no copy left there on Linux. HKDF leaves its working keys behind, the intermediate key it extracts and the key it derives, on the C stack and in memory it frees; IronDome cannot wipe those either, and overwrites them by deriving again from zeros. That rests on the library taking the same path through its code both times, which the tests check on every supported Python and IronDome does not control. A non-ASCII master password is normalised with Python's unicodedata before any of this, and unicodedata frees its own working copies of the text, as 4-byte code points, without overwriting them: the review found three copies of nearly all of a 3,600-byte one on Linux with Python 3.13, and none with 3.9; the two strings IronDome makes for it are zeroed in place on CPython. Decrypted entries are ordinary Python strings for as long as a command runs. Session and grant tokens are bearer secrets that live in your shell's environment by design. The recovery key is text you are shown once and may type back: as text it is an ordinary Python string, not locked memory, for as long as a command holds it. Locking the pages is best effort: where the system refuses it (a low RLIMIT_MEMLOCK, for one), the keys are still kept outside the Python heap and overwritten, but could be written to swap, and `irondome doctor` warns. A process with debugger rights over a running IronDome can read anything.

claims.title: Names, usernames, URLs and tags are encrypted, not just passwords
claims.statement: No entry name, username, URL, tag, alias, note or password appears in the vault file, its snapshots or the audit log. Record sizes are padded so they do not reveal password lengths.
claims.boundary: Visible to anyone who can read the file: how many entries there are and the padded size of each, when the vault was created and how many times it has been written, and how it opens (the kind, label, backend and Argon2id cost of each keyslot). The snapshots show which records changed with each write. Beside the vault, in clear: each session and grant file in `caps/` shows which of the two it is, when it was made, when it expires, how many uses are left, its label and the device key it is bound to, and `irondome grant ls` prints these without the master password; each line of `audit.log` shows a sequence number, a time and which key wrote it (the vault's, or a grant's id). A label is yours to choose: put nothing in it that you would not show.

claims.title: Altered, swapped or rolled-back records are rejected
claims.statement: Every record is authenticated with AES-256-GCM and bound to its vault, its entry and its revision. Changing a byte, moving a record to another entry, or restoring an older version of one record makes the vault refuse to read it.
claims.boundary: Replacing the whole file with an older copy of the whole file is not detected.

claims.title: Argon2id and AES-256-GCM, from one widely used library
claims.statement: Master passwords are stretched with Argon2id (by default 256 MiB, 3 passes and 4 lanes, and 64 MiB, RFC 9106's low-memory choice, on a machine with less than 3 GiB of RAM; never below the OWASP minimum), applied to a 32-byte HKDF-SHA256 prehash of the password and never to the password itself, keys are derived with HKDF-SHA256 and data is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using random 96-bit nonces. IronDome implements no primitive itself; all of them come from pyca/cryptography and are checked against published test vectors.
claims.boundary: No independent party has audited IronDome's use of these primitives. IRONDOME_KDF_MEMORY_MIB in the environment, or --kdf-memory-mib when a vault is made, replaces the default memory cost with any value from 19 MiB to 4 GiB; a cost the machine has no memory for is refused with an error when a vault is made or opened. `init`, `bunker create` and `status` show the cost and say when it is below the default; `export` warns.

claims.title: IronDome cannot make a network connection
claims.statement: No module imports a networking library, and every command works with socket creation disabled. There is no account, no sync, no telemetry and no update check.
claims.boundary: Programs you start with `irondome run` are yours: they can use the network.

claims.title: One direct dependency
claims.statement: The package depends on the Python standard library and on `cryptography`, and on nothing else. The only native code is a Secure Enclave helper compiled on your machine from source shipped in the package.
claims.boundary: `cryptography` bundles OpenSSL and brings what it depends on itself: `cffi` and `pycparser`, and `typing-extensions` on Python 3.9 and 3.10.

claims.title: Every file is owner-only and every write is atomic
claims.statement: Every file IronDome creates is mode 0600 and every directory 0700 regardless of the process umask. The vault is replaced atomically: an interrupted write leaves the previous vault intact, and a concurrent writer is refused rather than overwritten.
claims.boundary: These are POSIX permissions: the files belong to your user account, so every program running as you, and root, can read them.

claims.title: A grant opens only what it names, for as long as it says
claims.statement: A grant token gives access to the values named when it was created and to nothing else, until it expires or its uses run out. A used-up or expired grant is destroyed, and its token no longer opens anything.
claims.boundary: A grant token is a bearer secret: whoever holds it, and can read the grant file, has what it grants. Expiry, use counts and revoking a single grant are enforced by IronDome and by deleting the grant's file, not by hardware: a process that can write the bunker's caps/ directory can copy the file before a use or a revoke and put it back, and the grant then works again until it expires. Every grant is bound to a device secret of this machine, and irondome rekey or nuke destroys it, which ends every grant, even one whose file was put back.

claims.title: A grant never contains the vault key, the master password or an OTP seed
claims.statement: A grant is a separate encrypted snapshot of the named values. It cannot be turned into access to the rest of the vault: it holds neither the vault key nor the master password. A grant for a one-time-password field contains only the codes valid during its lifetime, never the seed that generates them.
claims.boundary: A grant carries one key of its own, derived one-way from the vault key and good only for signing that grant's audit records. Sessions (`irondome unlock`) are different: a session token wraps the vault key and is meant for the owner's own shell only.

claims.title: Secrets used by an agent do not appear in its transcript
claims.statement: `irondome run` places secrets in the child process's environment, masks them in everything the child prints (as they are; in base64; in hex, run together or with a colon, a hyphen or a space between the bytes; percent-encoded as the common encoders write it, once or twice over; HTML-escaped; as a JSON string the way Python, JavaScript, Go and PHP write one; as a shell string between quotes or as bash's `printf %q` writes it; with its quotes doubled, as in CSV; and each line of a secret of several lines), and never passes a session or grant token to the child. The MCP server returns names, exit codes and masked output, not secret values.
claims.boundary: This prevents accidents, not intent: a command that deliberately transforms a secret before printing it defeats masking, and so does an encoding that is not on the list: base64 or hex folded over several lines, a dump laid out by `xxd` or `od`, compression, a part of the value, a third round of percent-encoding, another escaping style (bash writes a value that holds a control character as `$'...'`). The Go and PHP forms follow what those encoders' documentation says they write; they were not run here. A value shorter than 4 bytes is not masked, one shorter than 8 only as it is and not in its encodings, and a line of a secret of several lines only if it is one unbroken token of 20 bytes or more (a line of a key, not a line with spaces, and not the lines that open and close a PEM block); a short value is masked wherever those characters occur, which can show a reader where it is. A grant created with --reveal, or an entry marked `--agent reveal`, allows the value to be shown. With --timeout the command and the processes that descend from it are asked to stop, given three seconds, and killed; one that made itself a daemon is not found, and whatever a command leaves running keeps the values it was given. `irondome run` reads `.env.irondome` in the working directory without being asked and says which variables it takes from it, with -q as well. A file nobody named may only ask for a secret under the name its owner gave it (NAME=irondome://NAME, where NAME is an alias or an entry: what --env NAME does); if it sets anything as written, or points a variable at another entry or at a field, `irondome run` refuses until the file is named with --env-file, because no list of the variables that choose what code runs (PATH, LD_PRELOAD, LESSOPEN, MAKEFILES and many more) is complete, and a variable pointed at a field its author can guess (a user name, a URL) chooses as well as one set as written. In a directory someone else wrote, that file still decides which of your named secrets the command receives: read it first. The MCP server runs for as long as the agent's session, and the values it has used stay in its memory, as ordinary Python strings, until it exits.

claims.title: An agent cannot widen its own access
claims.statement: Without a terminal or the master password, IronDome refuses to create sessions, aliases or entries, to change keyslots, to export, and to read entries the owner has not marked for agents. The one thing an agent can ask for is a time-boxed, use-only grant for entries marked for agents (`irondome approve`), and only the owner's Touch ID creates it. Under a session alone, IronDome's commands refuse to create a grant that would outlive the session and to set what agents may do with an entry: both ask for the master password again.
claims.boundary: A session token unwraps the vault key. Whatever holds one can do everything the owner can for as long as the session lasts: read, change and delete entries, and make grants that expire no later than it does. Ending the session early (`irondome lock`) revokes the grants made under it, which carry its mark in their label. What the commands refuse under a session stops accidents and tools that only run `irondome`; a program that uses the token with its own code is not bound by it and can make a grant that outlives the session. Never let an agent inherit one; use grants. What is done under a session is recorded in the audit log as `session`, with or without a terminal, not as `owner`; `agent` in that log is a command that had no terminal and was given no master password (the MCP server, a Touch ID approval). A Touch ID prompt shows text chosen by the program that raised it: read it before you touch. Anything that runs as you can type wrong master passwords: on a TPM, a few of them put the chip into lockout and the vault refuses its owner too until the TPM forgives them (a locked TPM takes no new keyslot either: the recovery key gets the owner in meanwhile with a file-based device key, `IRONDOME_DEVICE_BACKEND=software irondome recovery use`, and `irondome rekey` moves the vault back onto the chip afterwards).

claims.title: Every agent access is recorded, and edits to the record are detected
claims.statement: Each use of a grant, a session or a Touch ID approval, and every change to the vault, is appended to an encrypted, hash-chained log. `irondome audit --verify` detects edited, reordered, forged and removed lines. A re-key sets the log aside and starts a new one; the old one stays readable and checkable with `irondome audit --archive`.
claims.boundary: Deleting the newest lines of the log, or the whole log, is not detected, and a grant holder who can write the file can replace the newest lines with records of its own. What reads an archived log is the audit key of the vault key it was written under; each re-key carries those keys forward in the new vault's encrypted index. A log archived by a vault that did not yet do so, or one from another vault, cannot be read. While a re-key that was stopped part way has not been finished, the log on disk is still the one written under the old vault key: `irondome audit --verify` says that it cannot be checked yet, not that it was altered, and `irondome rekey` sets it aside so that it can be.

claims.title: Several bunkers on one machine, each sealed from the others
claims.statement: Every bunker has its own vault key, master password, device secret, recovery key, sessions, grants and audit log. Opening one bunker, or holding a session or grant for it, gives no access to any other, and `irondome bunker rm` destroys one bunker's device secret without touching the rest.
claims.boundary: Bunkers separate vaults, not operating-system accounts: every bunker belongs to the same user account, so malware running as that user is in the same position against each of them.

claims.title: The recovery key opens the vault without the device
claims.statement: A 160-bit recovery key, shown once at setup and stored nowhere, opens a copy of the vault on any machine: `irondome recovery use` asks for it and gives the vault a new master password bound to that machine. A lost laptop, a dead chip, a changed fingerprint or a forgotten master password is not the end of your data.
claims.boundary: `irondome recovery use` is the one command that takes the key; it replaces every keyslot that needed the old device key or the old password, Touch ID keyslots included, and leaves the recovery key as it was. An old device key that is on the machine it runs on is destroyed, as `passwd` does, so another copy of the vault on that machine that still used it then opens only with the recovery key; one that is elsewhere, or cannot be reached, is left alone, and where it still exists the old master password still opens old copies of the vault file. This is the same property that lets a recovery key outlive `nuke`. Keep it offline, or create the vault with --no-recovery. `irondome recovery new` and `irondome recovery remove` re-key the vault, so the old key opens neither the vault as it is now nor anything stored in it later; a copy of the vault file made before then still opens with the old key and shows what it held then. On a machine whose TPM is in lockout, `irondome recovery use` cannot make a keyslot on the chip and says how to make a file-based one instead. `irondome recovery use` ends sessions and deletes snapshots; it does not revoke grants: one whose device key is still on the machine works until it expires (`irondome grant revoke --all`, or `irondome rekey`).

claims.title: A 3.x vault migrates completely, and the old vault is left alone
claims.statement: `irondome migrate` reads a 3.x vault in any of its three modes, writes every entry into a v4 vault, compares each migrated value with the original and only then reports success. The 3.x directory is not modified unless you ask for it to be destroyed after a clean verification.
claims.boundary: A 3.x vault without a master password opens with the key 3.x kept in the OS keychain. IronDome reads it with /usr/bin/security on macOS and secret-tool on Linux, and with nothing else: on Windows, or on a Linux without secret-tool, you give the key yourself (irondome migrate --legacy-key). A key the keychain hands over proves nothing about who is asking, so such a vault is migrated at a terminal, not with --password-stdin. Vaults written before the 3.x format (1.x, and the 2025 script's) are read as they are, without opening them in 3.2.2 first.

claims.title: No core dumps, and on Linux no debugger from your other programs
claims.statement: IronDome turns off core dumps for itself, and on Linux also marks itself non-dumpable, which stops other processes of the same user from attaching a debugger or reading its memory.
claims.boundary: Root, or a process with debugger rights over IronDome, can still read its memory. On macOS IronDome sets no equivalent of the non-dumpable flag: whether another program of yours may attach a debugger is up to macOS. IRONDOME_DEBUG=1 in IronDome's environment switches both off, and `irondome doctor` then says so; where the system refuses either change, IronDome runs without it.

claims.title: A copied secret is taken off the clipboard
claims.statement: --copy hands the value to the system's clipboard tool on its standard input, never as an argument, and clears the clipboard after the bunker's clipboard_clear_seconds (30 by default), but only if the clipboard still holds that value.
claims.boundary: Clearing is best effort: every program running as you can read the clipboard until then, clipboard managers or sync may keep their own copy, and if the clearing helper is stopped, or the computer sleeps through the delay, the value stays until something else is copied.

claims.title: Secrets never go on a command line
claims.statement: No command takes a secret value (a password, key, token, TOTP seed or custom field) as a command-line argument: values come from a hidden prompt, standard input or a file, so they reach neither your shell history nor the process list. IronDome hands them to the programs it runs itself (clipboard tools, the Secure Enclave helper, tpm2-tools) the same way.
claims.boundary: A secret you put on a command line yourself, in a here-string or an echo, is in your shell's history, and so are entry names, usernames, URLs, tags and notes given as options (use --note-stdin for a note that is secret). `irondome run` hands secrets to the program you name through its environment, which other processes running as you can read.
